content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore efficient xpath and xquery within XML Performance and Reliability. You will connect its syllabus topics to an inspectable example, check the expected result, and note tool/version limits.
content.why_it_matters: Efficient XPath and XQuery matters because XML workflows rely on explicit structure and predictable processing. The lesson helps you reason about narrowing selections, avoid a common misunderstanding, and make a result reproducible for another developer.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: XML throughput and reliability depend on document size, parser strategy, query shape, transformation design, and error recovery. Measure using representative data rather than assuming that one parser style is always fastest.

content_blocks.title: Connect the subtopics
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly covers: Narrowing selections; Avoiding redundant traversal; Query evaluation costs; Indexes in XML databases; Measuring and profiling queries. Treat these as connected parts of one workflow: define the structure, make the relevant assumptions explicit, and verify a result with a small known input.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Efficient XPath and XQuery
content_blocks.code:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

# Use for trusted input only; configure a hardened parser for untrusted data.
for _event, elem in ET.iterparse("large-catalog.xml", events=("end",)):
    if elem.tag == "product":
        process_record = elem.findtext("name")  # replace with application processing
        print(process_record)
        elem.clear()
content_blocks.expected_output: Product names are processed one record at a time without retaining every completed product subtree.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this example as text. Run it only in a processor that supports the shown language/version; the standard CodeLeaf playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only and does not execute XML, XSD, XPath, XSLT, XQuery, Python, or SQL. For large record-oriented documents, consider incremental processing and clearing processed subtrees. Bound input size and depth, validate early when appropriate, and design retries so reprocessing does not create duplicate downstream effects.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the sample to its exact starting state before each experiment. Change one element, attribute, expression, or constraint at a time, then compare the result with the expected behavior.
content_blocks.limitations: The file must exist and the function body must implement bounded processing. This is a streaming pattern for controlled input, not a complete hardened production parser.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a document is correct because it looks readable.
common_mistakes.why: Visual appearance does not prove well-formedness, schema validity, correct namespace handling, or application-level meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse and validate the document with the intended processor, then assert its meaning using a focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing specification features with processor support.
common_mistakes.why: A standard may define features that a specific runtime does not implement.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the version and feature support; test with the actual target processor.

common_mistakes.why: Missing values, wrong types, namespace differences, or boundary inputs can expose failures.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a valid case, an invalid case, and an edge case to the verification notes.
